q: Which vault type does Azure Site Recovery use?
exp: Azure Site Recovery is configured in a Recovery Services vault, the same vault type used for VM backup. Backup vaults are for newer workloads such as disks and blobs, and Key Vault and storage accounts aren't vaults for ASR.

q: For Azure-to-Azure disaster recovery, where should the Recovery Services vault be?
opts: In the TARGET (recovery) region, not the source region
exp: For Azure-to-Azure disaster recovery, put the Recovery Services vault in the target (recovery) region. If the source region fails, the vault and its settings are still available to run the failover. A vault in the source region could go down with it.

q: Compare the vault region rules: Azure Backup vs ASR (Azure-to-Azure).
opts: Backup: vault in the SAME region as the VM; ASR: vault in the TARGET region
exp: This is a common exam trap. Azure Backup needs the Recovery Services vault in the same region as the VMs it protects. Azure Site Recovery (Azure to Azure) needs the vault in the target region, so it survives an outage in the source region.

q: What does ASR create in the target region when you enable replication?
opts: A target resource group, VNet (or mapping), cache storage in the source region, and replica managed disks
exp: When you enable replication, ASR sets up a target resource group, a target VNet (or a mapping to one you choose) and replica managed disks in the target region, plus a cache storage account in the source region. Replication starts immediately; it doesn't wait for a failover.

q: Where does ASR temporarily store changes from source VMs before sending them to the target region?
opts: A cache storage account in the SOURCE region
exp: ASR first writes VM disk changes to a cache storage account in the source region, then sends them to the replica disks in the target region. Changes don't go straight into the vault, and Key Vault and Log Analytics aren't involved.

q: What's a recovery point in ASR?
opts: A point-in-time state of the replicated VM that you can fail over to (crash-consistent or app-consistent)
exp: A recovery point is a copy of a replicated VM's state at a point in time that you can fail over to. It can be crash-consistent (taken every 5 minutes) or app-consistent (taken at the interval you set). The replication policy controls how long they're kept.

q: How often does ASR create crash-consistent recovery points for Azure VMs?
exp: For Azure VMs, ASR creates a crash-consistent recovery point every 5 minutes. App-consistent points are created less often, at an interval you configure in hours. It isn't hourly, daily or weekly.

q: Which failover type do you use when the primary region is actually down?
exp: When the primary region is really down, run an unplanned failover to bring VMs up in the target region from a recovery point. Test failover is only for drills, cleanup removes test VMs, and planned failover is for orderly moves with no data loss when the source is still healthy.

q: Order the steps of a complete ASR DR cycle:
items: Fail over to the secondary region
Enable replication to the target region
Re-protect (reverse replication) to the original region
Fail back to the primary region
exp: First enable replication to the target region. In a disaster, fail over to the secondary region. Then re-protect, which reverses replication so the secondary replicates back to the original region. Finally fail back to the primary region when it's healthy (and re-protect again).

q: After a test failover is validated, what do you do?
opts: Run 'Cleanup test failover' to delete the test VMs
exp: After checking the test VMs, run 'Cleanup test failover' to delete the test VMs and related resources. Committing applies to real failovers, disabling replication stops protection, and deleting the vault removes everything.

q: After a real failover, what does 'Commit' do?
opts: Finalizes the failover; you can no longer change to a different recovery point
exp: After a real failover, Commit confirms it: you can no longer change to a different recovery point. It doesn't start replication (that's re-protect), delete the source VMs, or cancel the failover.

q: For a DR drill, which network should test-failover VMs connect to?
opts: An isolated VNet in the target region, not connected to production
exp: Test-failover VMs should connect to an isolated VNet in the target region that isn't connected to production. Otherwise duplicate VMs with the same names and IPs could clash with production. The VMs still need a network, and the source VNet is in the other region.

q: Failover options let you choose which recovery point?
opts: Latest (lowest RPO), Latest processed (lowest RTO), Latest app-consistent, or a custom point
exp: Failover lets you pick the recovery point: Latest (processes all pending data for the lowest data loss), Latest processed (fastest), Latest app-consistent (apps are consistent), or a custom point. It's a trade-off between RPO and RTO, not a single fixed option.

q: Which option gives the fastest failover (lowest RTO)?
exp: Latest processed fails over to the newest recovery point that ASR has already processed, so it doesn't wait for pending data to be processed. That gives the fastest failover (lowest RTO). Latest has lower data loss but takes longer, and app-consistent points are older.

q: What can a recovery plan include besides machine groups?
opts: Pre/post scripts, Azure Automation runbooks, and manual actions
exp: Besides ordered groups of machines, a recovery plan can run pre- and post-scripts, Azure Automation runbooks (for example to update DNS or a load balancer), and manual actions that pause until someone confirms them. Budgets, policies and locks aren't part of a recovery plan.

q: Several VMs must fail over to a shared, consistent recovery point (for example, multi-VM apps). Which setting?
exp: Multi-VM consistency puts VMs into a replication group, so they share crash-consistent and app-consistent recovery points and fail over to the same moment in time — important for multi-tier apps. Recovery plans control order, not consistency, and backup policies are for backup.

q: Can ASR replicate on-premises VMware VMs and physical servers to Azure?
opts: Yes — ASR supports VMware, Hyper-V, and physical servers to Azure
exp: ASR can replicate on-premises VMware VMs, Hyper-V VMs and physical Windows or Linux servers to Azure, as well as Azure VMs between regions. It isn't limited to Azure VMs, Hyper-V or Linux.

q: Replicated VMs should come up in a specific availability zone in the target region. Is that configurable?
opts: Yes — you can choose target availability zones or sets in replication settings
exp: When you enable replication, you can choose target settings such as the availability zone or availability set the replicated VM uses in the target region. So the VM comes up in the zone you want after failover. This works for Windows and Linux and is set before failover.

q: Can ASR replicate VMs between availability zones in the SAME region?
opts: Yes — zone-to-zone disaster recovery is supported in many regions
exp: Yes. ASR supports zone-to-zone disaster recovery, replicating VMs from one availability zone to another in the same region, in many regions. It doesn't need Azure Backup, and it isn't only for VM scale sets.

q: How does ASR help keep RTO low for web apps after failover with DNS?
opts: Use recovery plan scripts or Traffic Manager to redirect users to the failed-over endpoints
exp: Plan for DNS and traffic redirection, for example with a recovery plan script or Traffic Manager priority routing.

q: Which ASR metric shows how current the replicated data is?
opts: RPO (replication health and RPO values per VM)
exp: Each replicated item shows its replication health and current RPO — how far the replica is behind the source — so you can see how current the data is. CPU and IOPS are performance metrics, and cost isn't a replication measure.

q: Which TWO are prerequisites for Azure-to-Azure replication?
opts: Outbound connectivity from source VMs to required Azure service endpoints/URLs (or service tags)
The latest Mobility service, installed automatically as an extension
exp: Source VMs need outbound connectivity to the Azure Site Recovery service URLs or service tags (for example through an NSG or proxy). The Mobility service is installed automatically as a VM extension when you enable replication and is kept updated. MARS and ExpressRoute aren't needed.

q: Answer Yes or No about ASR:
stmts: Re-protect reverses the replication direction after failover
ASR can be used to migrate VMs between regions
ASR replication costs are charged per protected instance
exp: Test failover doesn't interrupt replication; re-protect reverses it; migration is supported; ASR is billed per instance plus storage.

q: Ransomware encrypted a VM's files 3 days ago and they were replicated. Which service recovers clean data?
opts: Azure Backup (restore a recovery point from before the infection)
exp: ASR replicates changes within minutes, so the encrypted files are already in its recent recovery points (and it doesn't keep points for long). Azure Backup keeps older recovery points, so you can restore one from before the attack. That's why backups are your ransomware protection.

q: An app must run in another region within minutes of a regional outage, with minimal data loss. Which service?
exp: Azure Site Recovery keeps an up-to-date replica in another region, so the app can fail over within minutes (low RTO) with only a few minutes of data loss (low RPO). Restoring from Azure Backup is much slower. Blob versioning and templates don't replicate running VMs.

q: Which TWO are typical uses of Azure Backup rather than ASR?
opts: Long-term retention for compliance (for example, yearly points for 10 years)
Orchestrated regional failover with recovery plans
exp: Azure Backup is the tool for long-term retention (for example yearly points kept for 10 years) and for restoring a single deleted file or folder. Orchestrated regional failover with recovery plans, and continuous replication with a 5-minute RPO, are ASR features.

q: Which vault type protects Azure file shares?
exp: Azure file share backup is configured in a Recovery Services vault. Backup vaults handle disks, blobs and PostgreSQL, Key Vault stores secrets, and file shares can be protected, so 'None' is wrong.

q: Can you restore individual files from an Azure file share backup?
opts: Yes — full share restore or item-level (file/folder) restore to the original or an alternate location
exp: From an Azure file share backup you can restore the whole share or just specific files and folders, to the original location or to another one. MARS isn't involved, and restores go to Azure file shares, not on-premises.

q: When Azure Backup protects a file share, which protection does it add to the storage account?
opts: A resource lock to prevent accidental deletion of the account
exp: When you protect a file share, Azure Backup adds a delete lock to the storage account so nobody deletes it by accident — which would also delete the backups, since the snapshots live in the account. It doesn't enable immutable storage, private endpoints or GRS.

q: An ops team wants one dashboard showing VM CPU, failed backups, and storage availability. Best tool?
opts: Azure Monitor Workbooks (or a shared dashboard) combining metrics and log queries
exp: Azure Monitor Workbooks (or a shared dashboard) can combine metrics such as VM CPU and storage availability with log queries such as failed backup jobs into one view for the team. Advisor gives recommendations, the Activity log shows operations, and Cost analysis shows spend.

q: An admin must be alerted when anyone creates a role assignment at subscription scope. How?
opts: An activity log alert on the Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write operation
exp: Creating a role assignment is a control-plane operation (Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write) recorded in the Activity log. An Activity log alert on that operation at subscription scope fires every time it happens. Metric alerts watch numbers, and Advisor and budgets don't track role changes.

q: Which Azure Advisor category flags VMs that lack backup?
exp: Azure Advisor's Reliability category (formerly 'High availability') includes recommendations such as enabling backup on VMs. Cost, Performance and Security cover other areas.

q: You must check that every VM in a subscription has backup enabled, and enable it automatically. Best approach?
opts: Azure Policy: 'Configure backup on VMs...' with DeployIfNotExists and remediation
exp: A built-in Azure Policy definition ('Configure backup on virtual machines…') uses DeployIfNotExists to enable backup on VMs automatically, and a remediation task fixes existing VMs. Manual checks don't scale, alerts only notify, and locks only prevent deletion.

q: Answer Yes or No:
stmts: Alerts can monitor Recovery Services vault backup failures
Metric alert rules are billed per time series monitored
Log Analytics data can be queried across multiple workspaces in one query
exp: All four are true. Backup failures raise Azure Monitor alerts. Service Health alerts are Activity log alerts and cost nothing. Metric alert rules are billed per time series they monitor. And KQL can query several workspaces at once with the workspace() function.

q: Which KQL query lists failed Azure Backup jobs from the last day (resource-specific tables)?
opts: AddonAzureBackupJobs | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d) and JobStatus == "Failed"
exp: With resource-specific diagnostic tables, backup job data goes to AddonAzureBackupJobs, so filter it on the last day and JobStatus == "Failed". Heartbeat holds agent heartbeats, Perf holds performance counters, and AzureActivity holds control-plane operations, not backup job results.

q: A disk's free space must trigger an alert when it's below 10%. Which signal source?
opts: A log search alert on guest perf data (collected by AMA) or a VM insights metric
exp: Free disk space is measured inside the guest OS, so platform metrics don't include it. Collect it with the Azure Monitor Agent (for example through VM insights) and alert with a log search alert on that performance data. The Activity log and Service Health don't have disk space data.

q: Which built-in feature gives recommended alert rules for a VM with one click?
opts: Recommended alert rules (VM 'Alerts' → Enable recommended alert rules)
exp: On a VM's Alerts page you can enable recommended alert rules — common metric alerts such as CPU, available memory and network — in one step, with your own thresholds and action group. Advisor gives recommendations, Policy enforces rules, and Workbooks are reports.

q: Which CLI command creates a metric alert for VM CPU > 80%?
opts: az monitor metrics alert create -g RG1 -n cpu80 --scopes <vmId> --condition "avg Percentage CPU > 80" --action ag1
exp: az monitor metrics alert create sets the scope (--scopes with the VM's ID), the condition ("avg Percentage CPU > 80") and the action group (--action). The other commands don't exist, and az monitor log alerts are for log search queries.

q: Which CLI command creates an action group with an email receiver?
opts: az monitor action-group create -g RG1 -n ag1 --action email ops ops@contoso.com
exp: az monitor action-group create creates an action group, and each --action adds a receiver: here type email, name ops, address ops@contoso.com. The other commands don't exist.

q: What rate limits apply to action group notifications, such as SMS?
opts: SMS and voice are rate-limited (for example, no more than about 1 SMS every 5 minutes per number); email has higher limits
Webhooks are limited to 1 per day
exp: Action groups have rate limits per destination: no more than 1 SMS and 1 voice call every 5 minutes for each phone number, and up to 100 emails an hour per address. So notifications can be dropped during an alert storm. Webhooks aren't limited to one a day.

q: Autoscale settings, a feature of Azure Monitor, apply to which resources?
opts: VM scale sets, App Service plans, Cloud Services, and some others
exp: Autoscale in Azure Monitor works on resources that can add or remove instances, such as VM scale sets, App Service plans and Cloud Services (plus a few others, such as API Management). Storage accounts, VNets and Key Vault don't have instances to scale.

q: How can you be notified whenever autoscale adds or removes instances?
opts: Configure autoscale notifications (email/webhook) in the autoscale setting, or alert on the Autoscale activity log category
exp: In the autoscale setting you can send an email or call a webhook every time it scales in or out. Scale actions are also recorded in the Activity log under the Autoscale category, so you can alert on them. Advisor and Service Health don't report scale actions.

q: Which feature checks a public website's availability from multiple global locations?
exp: Application Insights availability tests (standard tests) send requests to a URL from several Azure locations around the world on a schedule and alert when it fails or is slow. IP flow verify and connection troubleshoot test from inside your network, and the Activity log records operations.

q: Which insights experience monitors Azure Kubernetes Service and container workloads?
exp: Container insights monitors AKS clusters (and Arc-enabled Kubernetes): node and pod performance, container logs and cluster health. VM insights monitors VMs, Network insights covers networking, and Storage insights covers storage accounts.

q: Order the steps to collect Windows event logs from 50 VMs and alert on critical events:
items: Create a log search alert on the Event table with an action group
Create a DCR for Windows event logs and associate it with the VMs (AMA installed)
Validate the data with a KQL query
exp: You need the workspace first, because the data collection rule sends data to it. Then create the DCR for Windows event logs and associate it with the 50 VMs (which installs AMA). Next, run a KQL query to confirm events are arriving, and finally create a log search alert on the Event table with an action group.

q: Can you back up a VM encrypted with Azure Disk Encryption?
opts: Yes — Azure Backup supports ADE VMs (with Key Vault permissions for the Backup service)
exp: Azure Backup supports VMs encrypted with Azure Disk Encryption on both Windows and Linux. The Backup service needs permissions on the Key Vault so it can back up the keys and secrets along with the encrypted disks. MARS isn't needed.

q: Backup of a VM fails with 'UserErrorGuestAgentStatusUnavailable'. What do you check first?
opts: That the VM agent is installed, running, and up to date, and the VM can reach Azure endpoints
exp: Azure VM backup works through the VM agent, which runs the backup extension. 'GuestAgentStatusUnavailable' means the agent isn't responding, so check that it's installed, running and up to date, and that the VM can reach Azure endpoints. Storage tier, port 445 and DNS zones aren't the cause.

q: Which restore type should you use to create a test copy of a VM from last week without touching the original?
exp: 'Create new VM' restores the recovery point as a separate VM, so the original keeps running unchanged. 'Replace existing' would overwrite the original's disks, and test failover is a Site Recovery feature, not a backup restore.

ctx: Requirements for a critical app VM in North Europe: (1) daily backups kept 7 years; (2) failover to West Europe within 30 minutes of a regional outage; (3) quarterly DR drills without impact; (4) restore of a single deleted folder.
q: Which combination meets ALL requirements?
opts: Azure Backup (daily policy plus yearly retention, file recovery) and ASR to West Europe (with test failovers)
exp: Azure Backup covers daily backups kept 7 years (yearly retention) and restoring a single folder (file-level recovery). Azure Site Recovery to West Europe covers failover within 30 minutes and quarterly drills without impact (test failover). Backup alone fails over too slowly, ASR alone can't keep 7 years or restore files, and blob features don't protect VMs.

ctx: Ops setup: LAW1 receives VM perf data (AMA/DCR) and vault diagnostics. Alert rules: metric CPU > 90% (AG-Ops), log alert on AddonAzureBackupJobs failures (AG-Backup). An alert processing rule suppresses notifications Saturdays 00:00–04:00.
q: Answer Yes or No:
stmts: A CPU spike at 02:00 on Saturday still creates a fired alert in Azure Monitor
AG-Ops sends an email for that 02:00 Saturday spike
Backup job failures can be alerted on through Log Analytics
Removing vault diagnostic settings would break the backup log alert
exp: Processing rules suppress actions, not the alert itself; the backup alert relies on diagnostics data in LAW1.
